The Kessler Syndrome (where blowups multiply exponentially) applied to software
items.summary: Earlier this year, inspired by a spate of supply chain attacks (like Mini Shai-Hulud-style worms, which culminated in headlines like Microsoft's Azure tools themselves being compromised), I wrote on my blog about the Kessler Syndrome, applied to software. Ie: the rising likelihood that, because of how bad actors with agentic AI can do far more damage, more quickly with the secrets they exfiltrate from penetrated networks, we could get into a situation where essentially every network of medium or greater complexity would become permanently "tainted" (never fully clean). Basically, can a swarm of agents 1) penetrate networks and exfiltrate secrets, 2) successfully install deeply embedded malware/rootkits, 3) move on to the next network, faster than hugops teams can rotate secrets and restore servers cleanly? For basically the entire existence of networked computers, this would have seemed a fantastical notion. But, throw in the current AI-fueled exploit discoveries and the countless servers vulnerable to RCEs across several stacks: I feel like the probability just keeps rising. Here are excerpts from my blog post, June 10: "'The Kessler Syndrome is a scenario where the density of objects and space debris in low Earth orbit becomes so high that collisions between them trigger a runaway chain reaction. Each crash generates thousands of new fragments, exponentially increasing the risk of further impacts and potentially rendering Earth’s orbit unusable.' "Just counting some of the high profile examples of public repos being laced with malware lately: Microsoft just disabled 70+ of their own repos, including Azure building tools. Repos from RedHat, tanstack, axios, Mistral, UiPath, and many other lower profile targets have been hacked. The list is long, and is much longer if you count companies (not just public repos for devs) that have been bitten, including names like GitHub, Cisco, OpenAI, and more. "...AIs or fancy new systems, probably made with AI appear to have dramatically lowered the amount of time to first utilization of stolen credentials. "It takes too long to clean an infected system/network (and the malware is getting much smarter/vindictive about detecting its removal, further complicating things), and it takes almost no time for a batch of stolen credentials to be exploited -> new networks traversed, leading to more secrets (that likely compromise more projects, rinse and repeat). "I think there is the very real possibility that we reach a Kessler Syndrome situation for shared/open source software, where the success of continued credential stealing campaigns permanently compromises medium, large, and even small networks, and lowers trust in shared software to a crippling degree." In just October: > Railway - customer secrets exposure > LiteLLM - malicious PyPI + Docker releases > Zeabur - infrastructure breached > OpenCode - AI API keys exposed > OVHcloud CLI - official binaries backdoored > Rank Math PRO - malware in official plugin > TeamUpdraft - customer data compromised > ConnectWise - cloud backup identities compromised > Tensorlake - npm package infected > PingCap - alleged major breach > SubQuery - backdoored npm package > GhostAction - GitHub repos with malicious workflows > PHP - critical RCE flaws > Node.js - security flaws patched > eMudhra - certificate authority keys compromised > Tailscale - eMudhra incident

Show HN: RMBG – remove backgrounds from images in the browser (no uploads)
items.summary: I am a person who does editing and digital designing. I used to use this tool, remove.bg, for getting transparent PNGs from either stock images or my own images. It was good, fast, free, and convenient. The only caveats for me were the export resolution limits and a privacy factor, that is, my images got uploaded to their servers. Recently, remove.bg announced that they are shutting down the standalone website and moving to inside Canva only. This really made me sad. I have been using this tool for a long time now. So, I made my own open-source tool, RMBG, which is: 1. Privacy-focused: the images never get uploaded somewhere; they stay and get processed only in your own browser. 2. No watermark or export resolution limits. 3. Fully free and open source with an MIT licence. No sign-in or accounts needed. 4. You can batch process and export as ZIP. 5. You can edit the image after the automated background removal, like erase objects, restore areas, recompute, etc. There are many view modes—mask, split, etc. 6. You can export in PNG, WebP, JPEG, and, in most browsers, AVIF. Other notes: Behind the scenes, it uses the BiRefNet-lite AI model in ONNX through Transformers.js. Inference runs in a worker with WebGPU where available and a single-threaded WASM fallback. The first visit downloads the runtime and about 98 MB of model weights from CDNs (that's why the first visit might be slower); later visits usually reuse the browser cache, so it can be fast. There is minimal analytics, using only GoatCounter for small events such as page visits, successful inferences, and quality feedback. No image pixels, filenames, or dimensions are collected. I am looking for contributors and as much help and support as possible, so I would appreciate people trying it out and giving feedback. Any ideas, PRs, and issues will be greatly appreciated. I will be active on HN and will reply to comments here. Hope to see some support here! Links: 1. Website - https://velmet44.github.io/rmbg/ 2. Source code on GitHub - https://github.com/Velmet44/rmbg 3. GoatCounter public analytics dashboard - https://velmet.goatcounter.com/ 4. Demo image - https://velmet44.github.io/rmbg/sample-split.png
